response.query: Can RD at GDPpc eligibility cutoffs, staggered DiD, and shift-share IVs produce consistent causal estimates of funding effects on regional TFP?
response.answer: RD at GDPpc cutoffs, staggered DiD, and shift-share IVs can produce consistent causal estimates of funding effects on regional TFP. These methods help address endogeneity and selection biases. They are effective in isolating treatment effects.

I'm working on a causal inference problem where I’d like to use a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) approach. Treatment: Changes in tariffs on certain commodities (these vary in magnitude — i.e., continuous treatment — and can occur multiple times for the same commodity/country). Staggered treatment timing, as tariff changes occur at different points in time for different units. Continuous treatment, since tariff changes are not binary (e.g., +5%, -10%). Multiple treatments, as units may receive more than one tariff change over time. results.title: Supplemental Security Income and Child Outcomes: Evidence from Birth Weight Eligibility Cutoffs | NBER
results.content:
Title: Supplemental Security Income and Child Outcomes: Evidence from Birth Weight Eligibility Cutoffs | NBER
# Supplemental Security Income and Child Outcomes: Evidence from Birth Weight Eligibility Cutoffs. We examine whether income transfers in the form of Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments for children with disabilities can help close the gap in outcomes due to this initial health and environmental disadvantage. We exploit a discontinuity in SSI eligibility at 1200 grams and use a regression discontinuity approach to produce causal estimates of the effects of SSI eligibility. We find that eligibility increases disability benefit participation, improves child outcomes and parenting behaviors, and shifts maternal labor supply from full to part time. results.title: The Causal Effects of an Industrial Policy | NBER
results.content:
Title: The Causal Effects of an Industrial Policy | NBER
# The Causal Effects of an Industrial Policy. Business support policies designed to raise productivity and employment are common worldwide, but rigorous micro-econometric evaluation of their causal effects is rare. We exploit multiple changes in the area-specific eligibility criteria for a major program to support manufacturing jobs ("Regional Selective Assistance"). Area eligibility is governed by pan-European state aid rules which change every seven years and we use these rule changes to construct instrumental variables for program participation. We match two decades of UK panel data on the population of firms to all program participants. IV estimates find positive program treatment effect on employment, investment and net entry but not on TFP. OLS underestimates program effects because the policy targets underperforming plants and areas. The positive program effect is not due to substitution between plants in the same area or between eligible and ineligible areas nearby. We estimate that "cost per job" of the program was only $6,300 suggesting that in some respects investment subsidies can be cost effective. We would like to thank the Department of Business and Innovation for data access and Paul David, Fernando Galindo-Rueda, Pete Klenow, Enrico Moretti, Beatrice Parrish, Marjorie Roome, David Southworth and Alex Wilson for useful insights.
